etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pees, pes, pais, borrowed from Anglo-Norman peis and Old French pais (“peace”), from Latin pāx (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to fasten, stick, place”), related to Latin pacīscor (“agree, stipulate”), Latin pangō (“fasten, fix”); see pact. Displaced native Old English sibb and friþ.

definitions.definition: A state of tranquility, quiet, and harmony; absence of violence.

quote.text: Naomi boasted in nothing but the God of Israel. And she found peace even in the midst of chaos when she went to Him in prayer.

definitions.definition: A state free of oppressive and unpleasant thoughts and emotions.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXXIV, page 53:
quote.text: ’Twere best at once to sink to peace,⁠Like birds the charming serpent draws,⁠To drop head-foremost in the jawsOf vacant darkness and to cease.

definitions.definition: A state free of war, in particular war between different countries.

quote.citation: 1969 March 31, John Lennon, Bagism Press Conference at Sacher Hotel, Vienna
quote.text: Now, a lot of cynics have said, “Oh, it’s easy to sit in bed for seven days,” but I’d like some of them to try it, and talk for seven days about peace. All we’re saying is give peace a chance.

quote.citation: 1993, Mark Berry as "King Harkinian", a character in Animation Magic, Link: The Faces of Evil, Philips Interactive Media (publ.).
quote.text: My boy, this peace is what all true warriors strive for.

quote.citation: 1996, Oliver Lindsay, Once a Grenadier: The Grenadier Guards 1945-1995, page 374:
quote.text: An uneasy peace descended upon Northern Ireland when the IRA agreed to a ceasefire in August 1994.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Old soldiers?”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine. […] One thing that is true, though, is that murder rates have fallen over the centuries, as policing has spread and the routine carrying of weapons has diminished. Modern society may not have done anything about war. But peace is a lot more peaceful.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Shut up!, silence!; be quiet, be silent.

quote.citation: 1846 October 1 – 1848 April 1, Charles Dickens, Dombey and Son, London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Hark!” said the old woman, triumphantly. “I hear a step coming.  […]  Do you hear him?”“I believe you are right, mother,” replied Alice, in a low voice. “Peace! open the door.”

quote.citation: 1882, Mark Twain, chapter 6, in The Prince and the Pauper:
quote.text: "Peace, my lord, thou utterest treason! Hast forgot the king's command? Remember I am party to thy crime, if I but listen."

definitions.definition: To make peace; to put at peace; to be at peace.

quote.citation: 1997, Yusuf Jah, Shah'Keyah Jah, Uprising, page 49:
quote.text: Within every hood they have to be peacing with themselves. Then when you're living in peace with yourself, [...]

quote.citation: 2006, Wayne Grady, Bringing back the dodo: lessons in natural and unnatural history:
quote.text: In another northern species, ptarmigan, such a see-saw pattern between warring and peacing has indeed been observed by researchers.
